The '''66th Academy Awards''' ceremony, organized by the [[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]] (AMPAS), honored [[1993 in film|films released in 1993]] and took place on March 21, 1994, at the [[Dorothy Chandler Pavilion]] in [[Los Angeles]] beginning at 6:00&nbsp;p.m. [[Pacific Time Zone|PST]] / 9:00&nbsp;p.m. [[Eastern Time Zone|EST]]. During the ceremony, AMPAS presented [[Academy Awards]] (commonly referred to as Oscars) in 23 categories. The ceremony, televised in the United States by [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]], was produced by [[Gilbert Cates|Gil Cates]] and directed by [[Jeff Margolis]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Credits |url=http://jeffmargolisproductions.com/credits/ |publisher=Jeff Margolis Productions |access-date=October 4, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131005000932/http://jeffmargolisproductions.com/credits/ |archive-date=October 5, 2013 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=66th Annual Academy Awards Presentation |url=https://www.nytimes.com/tv/show/38901/66th-Annual-Academy-Awards-Presentation/credits |access-date=December 5, 2013 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140118063507/http://www.nytimes.com/tv/show/38901/66th-Annual-Academy-Awards-Presentation/credits |archive-date=January 18, 2014 }}</ref> Actor [[Whoopi Goldberg]] hosted the show for the first time.<ref>{{cite news|title=Goldberg To Replace Crystal As Academy Awards Host |url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1994/02/07/goldberg-to-replace-crystal-as-academy-awards-host/ |access-date=December 5, 2013 |work=[[Orlando Sentinel]] |publisher=[[Tribune Publishing]] |date=February 7, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140103183157/http://articles.orlandosentinel.com/1994-02-07/news/9402070032_1_year-academy-academy-awards-oscar |archive-date=January 3, 2014 }}</ref> Nearly a month earlier in a ceremony held at [[The Beverly Hilton]] in [[Beverly Hills, California]] on February 26, the [[Academy Award for Technical Achievement|Academy Awards for Technical Achievement]] were presented by host [[Laura Dern]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Past Scientific & Technical Awards Ceremonies|url=http://www.oscars.org/awards/scitech/pastawards.html|access-date=July 31, 2013|work=[[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]]|publisher=AMPAS|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140213185729/http://www.oscars.org/awards/scitech/pastawards.html|archive-date=February 13, 2014}}</ref>

''[[Schindler's List]]'' won seven awards, including [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Eller |first=Claudia |title='Schindler's List' Brings Triumph for Spielberg : Movies: Director wins for best picture. Tom Hanks is honored as best actor and Holly Hunter is best actress. |url= https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-03-22-mn-37067-story.html |access-date=December 22, 2023 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=March 22, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20231222071320/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-03-22-mn-37067-story.html |archive-date= December 22, 2023 }}</ref> Other winners included ''[[Jurassic Park (film)|Jurassic Park]]'' and ''[[The Piano]]'' with three awards, ''[[Philadelphia (film)|Philadelphia]]'' with two, and ''[[The Age of Innocence (1993 film)|The Age of Innocence]]'', ''[[Belle Époque (film)|Belle Époque]]'', ''[[Defending Our Lives]]'', ''[[The Fugitive (1993 film)|The Fugitive]]'', ''[[I Am a Promise: The Children of Stanton Elementary School]]'', ''[[Mrs. Doubtfire]]'', ''[[Schwarzfahrer]]'', and ''[[The Wrong Trousers]]'' with one. The telecast was watched by more than 46 million viewers in the United States.

==Winners and nominees==
<!-- Please do not add any fact or statement below unless you have a credible source verifying it. Otherwise, it will be promptly removed. -->

The nominees for the 66th Academy Awards were announced on February 9, 1994, at the [[Samuel Goldwyn Theater]] in [[Beverly Hills, California]], by Academy president [[Arthur Hiller]] and actress [[Christine Lahti]].<ref>{{cite news |title=12 Oscar nominations for 'Schindler's List' |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=-jpOAAAAIBAJ&sjid=1xMEAAAAIBAJ&pg=4396,77565 |access-date=December 7, 2013 |work=[[New Straits Times]] |publisher=[[Media Prima]] |date=February 11, 1994 |archive-date=March 3, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230303002605/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=-jpOAAAAIBAJ&sjid=1xMEAAAAIBAJ&pg=4396,77565 |url-status=live }}</ref> ''[[Schindler's List]]'' led all nominees with twelve nominations; ''[[The Piano]]'' and ''[[The Remains of the Day (film)|The Remains of the Day]]'' tied for second with eight.<ref>{{cite news |last=Fox |first=David J. |title=Oscar's Favorite 'List' : The Nominations : 'Schindler's' Sweeps Up With 12 Nods : 'The Piano' and 'The Remains of the Day' both receive eight nominations; 'Fugitive,' 'In the Name of the Father' earn seven |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-02-10-ca-21449-story.html |access-date=November 25, 2013 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=February 10, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203080052/http://articles.latimes.com/1994-02-10/entertainment/ca-21449_1_oscar-nominations |archive-date=December 3, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Weinraub |first1=Bernard |title='Schindler' Nominated for 12 Oscars |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/02/10/arts/schindler-nominated-for-12-oscars.html |access-date=October 22, 2014 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=February 10, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141028115127/http://www.nytimes.com/1994/02/10/arts/schindler-nominated-for-12-oscars.html |archive-date=October 28, 2014}}</ref>

The winners were announced during the awards ceremony on March 21, 1994. Best Director nominee [[Jane Campion]] became the second woman to be nominated in that category.<ref>{{cite news |last=Fox |first=David J. |title='Schindler's' Adds a Pair to the List : Awards: Spielberg epic takes more honors--for screenwriting and editing. Jane Campion's 'The Piano' also wins. |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-03-14-ca-33988-story.html |access-date=October 21, 2013 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=March 14, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131024101413/http://articles.latimes.com/1994-03-14/entertainment/ca-33988_1_jane-campion |archive-date=October 24, 2013}}</ref> [[Holly Hunter]] and [[Emma Thompson]]'s nominations in both lead and supporting acting categories marked the first, and so far, only occurrence that two performers earned [[List of actors nominated for multiple Academy Awards in the same year|double acting nominations in the same year]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Brennan |first=Judy |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-02-11-ca-21862-story.html |title=The Hollywood Buzz on Oscar Snubs and Surprises |access-date=December 7, 2013 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=February 11, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131218102340/http://articles.latimes.com/1994-02-11/entertainment/ca-21862_1_oscar-nominations |archive-date=December 18, 2013}}</ref> Best Supporting Actress winner [[Anna Paquin]] became the first [[Millennials|Millennial]] member to win an Academy Award and, at age 11, the second youngest winner of a competitive acting Oscar, behind [[Tatum O'Neal]], who won at age 10 for ''[[Paper Moon (film)|Paper Moon]]'' (1973).<ref>{{cite news |last=Johnson |first=Allan |title=Anna Steals The Show |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1994/03/29/anna-steals-the-show/ |access-date=October 21, 2013 |work=[[Chicago Tribune]] |publisher=[[Tribune Media]] |date=March 29, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131021181400/http://articles.chicagotribune.com/1994-03-29/features/9403290026_1_piano-new-zealand-actress-award |archive-date=October 21, 2013}}</ref>

==Ceremony information==
[[File:Whoopi Goldberg Cannes 1992.jpg|thumbnail|upright|[[Whoopi Goldberg]] hosted the 66th Academy Awards.|alt=Headshot of Whoopi Goldberg. She has thick black hair and is wearing large hoop earrings.]]

Due to the negative reception received from the [[65th Academy Awards|preceding year's ceremony]], actor [[Billy Crystal]] announced that after overseeing four consecutive Oscar ceremonies, he would not be hosting the 1994 telecast.<ref>{{cite news|title=Company Town Annex |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-01-21-fi-14034-story.html |access-date=December 7, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=January 21, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131218082408/http://articles.latimes.com/1994-01-21/business/fi-14034_1_hosted-crystal-years |archive-date=December 18, 2013 }}</ref> In a statement released by his publicist, he stated, "After three [[Grammy]]s, four Oscars and six ''[[Comic Relief]]s'', I'm going to take a break from my hosting duties. I always felt honored to host the show and did my best to carry on the tradition of [[Bob Hope]] and [[Johnny Carson]]. I hope the new host has as good a time as I did."<ref>{{cite news|title=Billy Crystal Decides Not to Be Oscars Host |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/01/21/arts/billy-crystal-decides-not-to-be-oscars-host.html |access-date=December 7, 2013 |work=The New York Times |date=January 21, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131014003159/http://www.nytimes.com/1994/01/21/arts/billy-crystal-decides-not-to-be-oscars-host.html |archive-date=October 14, 2013 }}</ref> With Crystal absent to host the Oscars, many media outlets wondered whom producer [[Gil Cates]] would hire to emcee the program. Film columnist Jack Matthews suggested that actor [[Tom Hanks]], who would eventually win Best Actor for ''[[Philadelphia (film)|Philadelphia]]'', should host the show writing that he "has charm, dignity, wit, intelligence and, it's worth mentioning, he's a movie star!"<ref name=HostingRole>{{cite news|last=Matthews |first=Jack |title=Commentary: Who Will Host the Oscars? It's Not Crystal Clear |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-01-22-ca-14265-story.html |access-date=December 7, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=January 22, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131218102251/http://articles.latimes.com/1994-01-22/entertainment/ca-14265_1_oscar-host |archive-date=December 18, 2013 }}</ref> Cates also offered the role to performers [[Steve Martin]], [[Bette Midler]], and [[Johnny Carson]], but they all turned down the opportunity.<ref name=HostingRole/>

After several days of speculation, Cates announced that he hired Oscar-winning actress and comedian [[Whoopi Goldberg]] to host the festivities for the first time.<ref>{{cite news|title=Whoopi Goldberg To Play Host at Oscars |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/02/07/arts/whoopi-goldberg-to-play-host-at-oscars.html |access-date=December 7, 2013 |work=The New York Times |date=February 7, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131220231708/http://www.nytimes.com/1994/02/07/arts/whoopi-goldberg-to-play-host-at-oscars.html |archive-date=December 20, 2013 }}</ref> By virtue of her selection, Goldberg became both the first [[African American]] to host as well as the first woman to host the telecast solo.<ref>{{cite news|title=Comedian Whoopi Goldberg to Host Oscars|work=[[The Gazette (Montreal)|The Gazette]]|publisher=[[Postmedia Network]]|date=February 7, 1994|page=F5}}</ref> In an interview with the ''Los Angeles Times'', Cates explained the decision to hire her saying, "She is a highly recognizable star who has millions of fans."<ref>{{cite news|last=Fox |first=David J. |title=Whoopi! There It Is: Goldberg to Host Oscars : Awards: Performer breaks new ground - first woman and first African American as solo master of ceremonies. |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-02-07-ca-20044-story.html |access-date=December 7, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=February 7, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131218082916/http://articles.latimes.com/1994-02-07/entertainment/ca-20044_1_african-american-host |archive-date=December 18, 2013 }}</ref> He also addressed the media's concerns regarding Goldberg's raunchy and outspoken humor stating, "Some people may think she's potentially dangerous, and she says things that come to her mind. It's going to be exciting for me. The main thing is she wants to do it and she's smart. Whatever she says will be appropriate."<ref>{{cite news|last=Ryan|first=Desmond|title=Whoopi pushes the envelope|work=[[Austin American-Statesman]]|publisher=[[Cox Enterprises]]|date=March 20, 1994|page=7}}</ref> Goldberg expressed that she was thrilled to be selected to emcee the 1994 ceremony commenting, "To go from watching to winning to hosting in one lifetime is major."<ref>{{cite news|last=Marx |first=Andy |title=Goldberg set to host Oscarcast |url=https://variety.com/1994/film/news/goldberg-set-to-host-oscarcast-118072/ |access-date=December 7, 2013 |work=Variety |publisher=PMC |date=February 6, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131216223032/http://variety.com/1994/film/news/goldberg-set-to-host-oscarcast-118072/ |archive-date=December 16, 2013 }}</ref>

As with previous ceremonies he produced, Cates centered the show around a theme. This year, he christened the show with the theme "People Behind the Camera" commenting that "It will be a salute to those unseen men and women who make what we see on the screen, the artist and craftspeople responsible for the magic of the movies."<ref>{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=917}}</ref> In tandem with the theme, the ceremony's opening number featured a montage produced by [[Chuck Workman]] saluting the many individuals such as directors, editors, and composers who are involved in moviemaking. During that segment, singer [[Bernadette Peters]] performing a modified version of [[Stephen Sondheim]]'s song "Putting It Together" from his musical ''[[Sunday in the Park with George]]''.<ref>{{harvnb|Pond|2005|p=45}}</ref> Filmmaker and editor Carol A. Streit assembled another montage featuring a salute to the work of cinematographers and their contributions to film.<ref>{{cite news|title=The 66th Annual Academy Awards Presentation |url=http://www.hollywood.com/tv/55443482/the-66th-annual-academy-awards-presentation |access-date=December 7, 2013 |work=[[Hollywood.com]] |publisher=Hollywood.com, LLC |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131212090027/http://www.hollywood.com/tv/55443482/the-66th-annual-academy-awards-presentation |archive-date=December 12, 2013 }}</ref>

Several other people and elements were also involved with the production of the ceremony. Production designer Roy Christopher designed a new stage for the ceremony which prominently featured five giant Oscar statues each flanked inside metal cones that were illuminated recurrently throughout the show.<ref name="Oscar Time">{{cite news|last=Welkos |first=Robert W. |title=Oscar Time--Without a Safety Net : Welcome to Live TV--When Even Dogs Can Have Their Day |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-03-21-ca-36771-story.html |access-date=December 7, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=March 21, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131218082936/http://articles.latimes.com/1994-03-21/entertainment/ca-36771_1_oscar-time/2 |archive-date=December 18, 2013 }}</ref> Film composer and musician [[Bill Conti]] served as musical director of the ceremony.<ref>{{cite news|title=Conti to tune Awards |url=https://variety.com/1994/film/news/conti-to-tune-awards-117111/ |access-date=January 3, 2014 |work=Variety |publisher=PMC |date=January 3, 1994 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140104113409/http://variety.com/1994/film/news/conti-to-tune-awards-117111/ |archive-date=January 4, 2014 }}</ref> Dancer [[Debbie Allen]] choreographed a dancer number showcasing the Best Original Score nominees featuring eight prestigious ballet and dance troupes from around the world.<ref name=BalletDance/>

An [[in memoriam segment]] was introduced for the first time during the ceremony. In subsequent years, it became the permanent element of the Oscars.<ref>{{cite news|last=Cieply |first=Michael |author-link=Michael Cieply |title=Even for the Dead, There's a Race to Make the A-List at Oscars |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/02/08/movies/awardsseason/even-the-oscar-memorial-list-is-a-focus-of-campaigning.html |access-date=May 11, 2026 |work=The New York Times |date=February 7, 2013 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140612182338/http://www.nytimes.com/2013/02/08/movies/awardsseason/even-the-oscar-memorial-list-is-a-focus-of-campaigning.html |archive-date=June 12, 2014 }}</ref>

===Box office performance of nominees===
At the time of the nominations announcement on February 9, the combined gross of the five Best Picture nominees at the US box office was $261&nbsp;million, with an average of $52.2&nbsp;million per film.<ref name=BoxOfficeOscars>{{cite news|title=1993 Academy Award Nominations and Winner for Best Picture |url=https://boxofficemojo.com/oscar/chart/?yr=1993&p=.htm |access-date=November 25, 2013 |work=[[Box Office Mojo]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131202231138/http://boxofficemojo.com/oscar/chart/?yr=1993&p=.htm |archive-date=December 2, 2013 }}</ref> ''The Fugitive'' was the highest earner among the Best Picture nominees with $179&nbsp;million in domestic box office receipts.<ref name=BoxOfficeOscars/> The film was followed by ''Schindler's List'' ($29.6&nbsp;million), ''The Piano'' ($25.7&nbsp;million), ''The Remains of the Day'' ($19.5&nbsp;million), and finally ''In the Name of the Father'' ($6.5&nbsp;million).<ref name=BoxOfficeOscars/>

Of the top 50 grossing movies of the year, 36 nominations went to 14 films on the list. Only ''The Fugitive'' (3rd), ''The Firm'' (4th), ''Sleepless in Seattle'' (6th), ''In the Line of Fire'' (7th), ''Dave'' (13th), ''Philadelphia'' (29th), ''What's Love Got to Do With It'' (38th), and ''The Age of Innocence'' (49th) were nominated for directing, acting, screenwriting, or Best Picture.<ref name="boxofficemojooscars">{{cite web|url=https://boxofficemojo.com/yearly/chart/?asof=1994-02-08&view=releasedate&view2=domestic&yr=1993&sort=gross&order=DESC&p=.htm |title=1993 Domestic Grosses |work=Box Office Mojo |access-date=June 5, 2013 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131202223827/http://boxofficemojo.com/yearly/chart/?asof=1994-02-08&view=releasedate&view2=domestic&yr=1993&sort=gross&order=DESC&p=.htm |archive-date=December 2, 2013 }}</ref> The other top 50 box office hits that earned nominations were ''Jurassic Park'' (1st), ''Mrs. Doubtfire'' (2nd), ''Cliffhanger'' (9th), ''The Nightmare Before Christmas'' (24th), ''Addams Family Values'' (25th), and ''Beethoven's 2nd'' (27th).<ref name="boxofficemojooscars" />

===Critical reviews===
The show received a positive reception from most media publications. ''[[The New York Times]]'' film critic [[Janet Maslin]] raved that the telecast had "less silliness and less small talk, with more emphasis on cleverly chosen film clips and the bona fide Hollywood magic being celebrated." She also praised host Goldberg saying that she "sustained a tone of levity, which became particularly important as the sweep by ''Schindler's List'' threatened to bring out great ponderousness in some quarters."<ref>{{cite news|last=Maslin |first=Janet |author-link=Janet Maslin |title=Critic's Notebook; Minus Suspense Factor, Oscars Cut to the Chase |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/03/23/movies/critic-s-notebook-minus-suspense-factor-oscars-cut-to-the-chase.html |access-date=November 25, 2013 |work=The New York Times |date=March 23, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131219142507/http://www.nytimes.com/1994/03/23/movies/critic-s-notebook-minus-suspense-factor-oscars-cut-to-the-chase.html |archive-date=December 19, 2013 }}</ref> ''[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]'' television critic Robert Bianco commended Goldberg's performance writing that "She never acted like she was too smart or to hip for the show she was hosting; she never smirked like there was a joke she alone was cool enough to get." He also extolled producer Cates by commenting, "In place of the extraneous jokes and terrible production numbers, he gave us a theme that worked and a generous selection of clips to back it up."<ref>{{cite news|last=Bianco|first=Robert|title=Telecast shines spotlight on movies, not distractions|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1129&dat=19940322&id=FHgxAAAAIBAJ&sjid=2W8DAAAAIBAJ&pg=3153,3920374|access-date=December 7, 2013|work=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]|publisher=[[Crain Communications]]|date=March 22, 1994|archive-date=July 19, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230719193820/https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1129&dat=19940322&id=FHgxAAAAIBAJ&sjid=2W8DAAAAIBAJ&pg=3153,3920374|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Anne Thompson (film critic)|Anne Thompson]] of ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' lauded Goldberg by stating, "Her elegant appearance (at least during the first half), her uncharacteristic restraint (she didn't cuss), and her ability to make it funny (despite the very somber speeches) made the ho-hum telecast worth watching."<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Thompson |first=Anne |author-link=Anne Thompson (film critic) |title=Oscar's List |url=https://ew.com/article/1994/04/01/what-happened-oscars/ |access-date=December 31, 2013 |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |publisher=[[Time Warner]] |date=April 1, 1994 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140101081310/http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0%2C%2C301647%2C00.html |archive-date=January 1, 2014 }}</ref>

Some media outlets were more critical of the show. Television critic [[Howard Rosenberg]] of the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' lamented that Goldberg's humor "wilted in a blessedly brief 3-hour-and-18-minute telecast." He also wrote that compared with Billy Crystal, her hosting skills were "balmy".<ref>{{cite news|last=Rosenberg |first=Howard |author-link=Howard Rosenberg |title=Calendar Goes to the OSCARS : Whoopi, Better Naughty Than Boring : Awards: Goldberg fails to hit a funny bone or stir up any of the controversy that was hyped the week before the telecast. In fact, her hosting is '' balmy'', particularly compared to predecessor Billy Crystal |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-03-22-ca-37195-story.html |access-date=December 7, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=March 22, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131022101725/http://articles.latimes.com/1994-03-22/entertainment/ca-37195_1_lorena-bobbitt-telecast-color-purple |archive-date=October 22, 2013 }}</ref> ''[[Orlando Sentinel]]'' film critic Jay Boyar bemoaned that "this year's Oscarcast was only a little more exciting than a wine snob droning on about his favorite vintages."<ref>{{cite news|last=Boyar |first=Jay |title=Oscar Show's Rating: Plenty Of Class, Not Much Excitement |url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1994/03/25/oscar-shows-rating-plenty-of-class-not-much-excitement/ |access-date=December 31, 2013 |work=Orlando Sentinel |publisher=Tribune Publishing |date=March 25, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140101214020/http://articles.orlandosentinel.com/1994-03-25/entertainment/9403240457_1_oscarcast-political-slogans-academy |archive-date=January 1, 2014 }}</ref> Harold Schindler of ''[[The Salt Lake City Tribune]]'' remarked that Whoopi's preference for "insider" jokes "left the audience murmuring and most viewers probably scratching their heads." He also added the biggest letdown of the telecast was "Goldberg's seeming ineptness at understanding the moment"<ref>{{cite news|last=Schindler|first=Harold|title=Spielberg shines at Oscars, but all that gliters isn't Goldberg|work=[[The Salt Lake City Tribune]]|publisher= [[MediaNews Group]] |date=March 23, 1994}}</ref>

===Ratings and reception===
The American telecast on ABC drew in an average of 46.26 million people over its length, which was a 1% increase from the [[65th Academy Awards|previous year's ceremony]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Johnson |first=Greg |title=Call It the Glamour Bowl |url=https://articles.latimes.com/1999/mar/18/business/fi-18458/2 |access-date=August 26, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=March 18, 1999 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130928053918/http://articles.latimes.com/1999/mar/18/business/fi-18458/2 |archive-date=September 28, 2013 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |first=Bill |last=Gorman |title=Academy Awards Averages 41.3 Million Viewers; Most Since 2005 |url=http://tvbythenumbers.com/2010/03/08/academy-awards-averages-41-3-million-viewers-most-since-2005/44217 |work=[[TV by the Numbers]] |publisher=[[Tribune Media]] |date=March 8, 2010 |access-date=March 12, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100310080531/http://tvbythenumbers.com/2010/03/08/academy-awards-averages-41-3-million-viewers-most-since-2005/44217 |archive-date=March 10, 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref> However, the show drew lower [[Nielsen ratings]] compared to the previous ceremony with 31.86% of households watching over a 49.28 share.<ref name="TVB Oscars">{{cite news|title=Academy Awards ratings |work=[[Television Bureau of Advertising]] |url=http://www.tvb.org/media/file/Academy_Awards.pdf |access-date=June 27, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130515152338/http://www.tvb.org/media/file/Academy_Awards.pdf |archive-date=May 15, 2013 }}</ref> It also drew a lower 18–49 demographic rating with a 19.73 rating over a 40.53 share among viewers in that demographic.<ref name="TVB Oscars" />

In July 1994, the ceremony presentation received seven nominations at the [[46th Primetime Emmy Awards|46th Primetime Emmys]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Primetime Emmy Award database |url=http://www.emmys.com/shows/66th-annual-academy-awards |access-date=October 1, 2013 |publisher=[[Academy of Television Arts and Sciences]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130926071736/http://www.emmys.com/shows/66th-annual-academy-awards |archive-date=September 26, 2013 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Emmy Award Nominations 1994 : Nighttime Nominees: A Complete Rundown |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-07-22-ca-18748-story.html |access-date=December 5, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=July 22, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131015032226/http://articles.latimes.com/1994-07-22/entertainment/ca-18748_1_nypd-blue |archive-date=October 15, 2013 }}</ref> Two months later, the ceremony won one of those nominations for Outstanding Technical Direction/Camera/Video for a Miniseries or Special (Averill Perry, Jim Ralston, Kenneth R. Shapiro, Bill Pope, Hector Ramirez, Larry Heider, Dave Levisohn, Blair White, Bill Philben, Ralph Alcocer, Larry Stenman, Bud Holland, David Irete, Tom Geren, Dale Carlson, David Plakos, Ted Ashton, Jeff Mydoc, Chuck Pharis, Jean M. Mason).<ref>{{cite news|title=The 46th Annual Emmy Awards: Who Won What: The List of Winners on TV's Annual Night of Nights |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-09-12-ca-37696-story.html |access-date=December 5, 2013 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=September 12, 1994 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131224092822/http://articles.latimes.com/1994-09-12/entertainment/ca-37696_1_nighttime-emmy-awards/2 |archive-date=December 24, 2013 }}</ref>

=="In Memoriam"==
The first annual "In Memoriam" tribute was presented by actress [[Glenn Close]]. The montage featured an excerpt of the main title of ''[[Terms of Endearment]]'' composed by [[Michael Gore]].<ref>{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=932}}</ref>
